# BSON Protocol

`BSON` ([bsonspec.org](https://bsonspec.org)) is implemented with a hybrid of the same shape as
`protocols/cbor.hpp`:

- **Writing** wraps `jsoncons::bson::bson_bytes_encoder` (`<jsoncons_ext/bson/bson.hpp>`), a
  SAX-style visitor with the same interface as `jsoncons::cbor::cbor_bytes_encoder` (already used
  by the CBOR backend) — `begin_array`/`begin_object`/`key`/`int64_value`/etc map almost one-to-one
  onto zerialize's `Writer` concept.
- **Reading** does **not** use jsoncons at all. `BsonDeserializer` is a hand-rolled, span-walking,
  zero-copy parser, matching the precedent `cbor.hpp` already set: jsoncons is linked in for its
  encoder, but `CborDeserializer` is independent of jsoncons' own DOM/cursor readers, for zero-copy
  laziness and full control over the `Reader` concept's random-access semantics. The same reasoning
  applies here. BSON's format makes this easier than CBOR's: no indefinite-length forms, no
  variable-width integers — every length is a plain little-endian `int32`/`int64`.

Implementation: `include/zerialize/protocols/bson.hpp`

BSON support shares its jsoncons dependency with CBOR (see `CMakeLists.txt`); enabling either
`ZERIALIZE_ENABLE_CBOR` or `ZERIALIZE_ENABLE_BSON` fetches it. Both default **on** — unlike BEVE,
this adds no new third-party dependency and no C++ standard bump.

## Wire format

A document (or array — same physical layout) is `int32 total_length (LE, self-inclusive)`
followed by elements, followed by a single `0x00` terminator byte. Each element is
`uint8 type | cstring name (NUL-terminated, no length prefix) | value`.

Relevant type tags (from `jsoncons_ext/bson/bson_type.hpp`, the reference this implementation's
constants are taken from directly rather than re-declared):

| tag | type | value encoding |
|---|---|---|
|`0x01`| double | 8 bytes IEEE-754 LE |
|`0x02`| string | `int32 length-incl-NUL \| bytes \| 0x00` |
|`0x03`| document | nested document (zerialize `map`) |
|`0x04`| array | same physical layout as document (zerialize `array`) |
|`0x05`| binary | `int32 payload_length \| uint8 subtype \| bytes` (zerialize `blob`) |
|`0x08`| bool | 1 byte |
|`0x0A`| null | (no payload) |
|`0x10`| int32 | 4 bytes LE |
|`0x12`| int64 | 8 bytes LE |

BSON arrays are, on the wire, documents whose element names happen to be the stringified indices
`"0","1","2",...` (confirmed in jsoncons' encoder: array elements get their key auto-generated by
an internal counter, never via an explicit `key()` call). This implementation never interprets
those name strings as integers — array indexing just walks elements positionally, both for writing
(the `Writer`'s `begin_array`/`key`-free element calls) and reading (`operator[](size_t)` counts
elements, ignoring what their name string says), which is also more robust against a
non-sequentially-keyed foreign BSON array.

Unlike CBOR/MsgPack/BEVE, a raw span of BSON *value* bytes does not self-identify its type — the
type tag lives once in the parent element's header, not repeated in the value bytes. So every
`BsonDeserializer` node explicitly carries the type byte it was constructed with (propagated from
whichever element header produced it), rather than recovering it by peeking bytes.

## Two format-inherent constraints

These are real limitations of BSON itself, confirmed by reading jsoncons' encoder source, not
implementation choices:

1. **No top-level scalar, and no way to tell a root array from a root document on read.**
   jsoncons' `visit_int64`/`visit_double`/etc. all refuse to write when there's no open
   document/array frame — BSON's top-level value must always be a document or array; writing a
   bare scalar (`serialize<Bson>(42)`) throws `SerializationError`. `RootSerializer::finish()`'s
   "nothing was ever written" fallback is an **empty document** (5 bytes: `05 00 00 00 00`), not
   `null` the way CBOR's is, since BSON has no top-level null.
   Writing a bare *array* at the root (`serialize<Bson>(zvec(...))`) does succeed, but a document
   and an array are physically identical on the wire — only a *parent* element's header records
   which one a value is, and the root has no parent. jsoncons' own `bson_parser` resolves this by
   always decoding the top level as a document (confirmed by reading it), and `BsonDeserializer`
   does the same for consistency. So a bare array root reads back with `isMap()==true`,
   `isArray()==false`, and its elements reachable as `v["0"]`, `v["1"]`, ... This only affects the
   absolute root — arrays nested anywhere below it keep a real type tag in their parent's element
   header and are unaffected. In practice this means: wrap arrays in a document key at the top
   level (`zmap<"items">(zvec(...))`), which is also the conventional way to use BSON/MongoDB
   documents anyway. Because of this, `test_zerialize.cpp` gives `Bson` its own DSL test coverage
   (`test_bson_specific()`) instead of running it through the shared `test_protocol_dsl<P>()` /
   `test_dynamic_serialization<P>()`, both of which include bare-array-root cases.
2. **No unsigned 64-bit wire type.** BSON only has `int32`, `int64`, and `double` — no `uint64`.
   jsoncons' `visit_uint64` throws for any value `> INT64_MAX` rather than silently truncating or
   reinterpreting bits; `Bson::Serializer::uint64()` lets that propagate as `SerializationError`.
   On the read side, since BSON can't distinguish "written via `int64()`" from "written via
   `uint64()`" for a value that fits in `int64`, `isInt()` is true for any int32/int64 node and
   `isUInt()` is *also* true when the decoded value is non-negative — the two are allowed to
   overlap, the same convention `msgpack.hpp` already uses for small values. `translate.hpp`'s
   `write_value()` checks `isInt()` before `isUInt()`, so this doesn't change cross-protocol
   translation behavior.

## Known v1 limitations

MongoDB-specific tags with no equivalent in zerialize's data model — `object_id` (`0x07`),
`datetime` (`0x09`), `regex` (`0x0B`), `javascript`(`_with_scope`) (`0x0D`/`0x0F`), `symbol`
(`0x0E`, deprecated by the spec itself — read as a string, like jsoncons does), `timestamp`
(`0x11`), `decimal128` (`0x13`), `min_key`/`max_key` (`0xFF`/`0x7F`) — are correctly *skipped* (so
traversing an array or document containing one doesn't break), but not readable as scalars.

Binary subtype is not exposed: `binary()` always writes subtype `0x00` ("generic binary", the
spec's conventional choice — jsoncons' own tag-less `byte_string_value()` overload defaults to
`0x80` instead, which we deliberately override for interop), and `asBlob()`/`isBlob()` accept any
subtype on read.

## Interop and translation

Bson implements the same `Reader`/`Writer` surface as the other protocols:

- Serialize with `serialize<zerialize::Bson>(...)`
- Translate to/from other protocols with `translate<OtherProto>(bson_reader)` /
  `translate<zerialize::Bson>(other_reader)`
